edges.effect_quant: The largest updated meta-analysis of 37 cohorts involving 2,258,029 participants found a pooled relative risk of 0.55 for top versus bottom fitness tertiles and 0.89 per 1-MET higher fitness; the earlier JAMA meta-analysis found a 1.70 relative risk of all-cause mortality for low versus high cardiorespiratory fitness.
edges.population: generally healthy adults undergoing exercise-based cardiorespiratory fitness assessment
edges.mechanism: Low VO2max behaves partly as low cardiopulmonary reserve and partly as a summary marker for lower physical activity, sarcopenia, metabolic dysfunction, and autonomic vulnerability. That makes the pathway to higher mortality broad rather than disease-specific, which is why the most credible effect is on total mortality rather than one isolated cause.
edges.summary: This is one of the cleaner prognostic fitness edges in the graph. Across large cohort meta-analyses, lower cardiorespiratory fitness consistently tracks with higher all-cause mortality, and the argument is mostly about slope and threshold rather than about whether the relationship is real.
edges.caveats: The evidence is observational, so residual confounding by smoking, adiposity, illness burden, and long-term physical activity patterns never fully disappears. Still, the signal is unusually consistent across cohorts, fitness-testing methods, and demographic subgroups.

evidence.notes: Cardiorespiratory fitness as a quantitative predictor of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events in healthy men and women: a meta-analysis.
Objectively Assessed Cardiorespiratory Fitness and All-Cause Mortality Risk: An Updated Meta-analysis of 37 Cohort Studies Involving 2,258,029 Participants.

evidence.citation: Steell L 2019 Br J Sports Med

new_entities.name: Low cardiorespiratory fitness
new_entities.description: Cardiorespiratory fitness low enough to place an adult near the bottom of age- or sex-adjusted aerobic capacity distributions, typically measured or estimated from exercise testing.
